"The Debt We Owe: A Case for Reparative Justice"

Ladies and gentlemen,

Let me begin with a simple truth we have spent centuries avoiding: neutrality in the face of compounded injustice is not justice. It is abandonment.

We stand in a nation built — literally, physically built — by the labor of stolen people. For 246 years, Black men and women worked fields they could not own, built wealth they could not hold, and raised children they could not protect. And when slavery ended, the theft did not end. It evolved. Black Codes. Convict leasing. Jim Crow. Redlining. Mass incarceration. Each generation invented new architecture for the same old house of exclusion.

And what was our answer? We said, "Let us now be colorblind."

Think about the audacity of that. Centuries of race-conscious oppression met with the suggestion that race-conscious repair is somehow the real injustice. We used race to create the wound, then declared it impermissible to use race to heal it.

This is not a debate about preference. This is a debate about debt.

The Mathematics of Injustice

Let me speak plainly about what was taken.

Economists have estimated the value of uncompensated slave labor between $14 and $20 trillion in today's dollars. That is not a metaphor. That is stolen capital — capital that built industries, universities, and generational wealth for white families while Black families began freedom with nothing.

But slavery was only the beginning of the ledger.

The Homestead Act distributed 270 million acres of land — nearly 10 percent of the entire nation — almost exclusively to white families. The FHA and the GI Bill, the greatest wealth-building programs in American history, were administered in ways that systematically excluded Black veterans and Black homebuyers. While white suburbia flourished on government subsidy, Black neighborhoods were literally outlined in red and starved of investment.

Today, the median white family holds roughly eight times the wealth of the median Black family. The Black unemployment rate has been approximately double the white rate for every single year it has been measured — in boom times and in recessions, under Democrats and Republicans, in war and in peace.

These are not gaps. They are monuments to policy. They were built intentionally, and they will not dismantle themselves through patience or goodwill.

Why Race-Neutral Solutions Are Not Enough

I hear the objection already. "Address poverty. Address class. Help everyone who is disadvantaged."

I am not opposed to universal programs. But let me tell you why they are insufficient standing alone.

Race-neutral programs applied to race-specific damage produce race-specific neglect. When you poison one well and then announce clean water for everyone, the people drinking from the poisoned well do not catch up. They fall further behind, because their need was particular, and your remedy was general.

Studies have shown this repeatedly. Race-neutral anti-poverty programs reduce poverty across the board, yes — but they do not close racial gaps, because those gaps were not caused by class alone. They were caused by race. By policy. By design.

You cannot repair what you refuse to name.

The Moral Case

Now let me address the moral core of this argument, because I know many people feel discomfort when we speak about explicitly favoring one group.

I understand that discomfort. I ask you to sit with it. And then I ask you to compare it to the discomfort of a Black family in 2024 who has done everything right — worked hard, stayed in school, followed every rule this society prescribed — and still holds a fraction of the wealth, still faces discrimination in hiring, housing, lending, and healthcare, still watches their children treated as threats before they are treated as children.

Which discomfort should move us to action?

Explicit, sustained, race-conscious investment in Black communities is not reverse discrimination. It is correction. When a court finds that a company stole from a specific victim, it does not order the company to be nicer to everyone. It orders restitution to the victim. That is not favoritism. That is justice.

And we know this intuitively in every context except race. If a hurricane devastates one city, we do not distribute aid equally to all cities. We send aid where the damage is. If a doctor discovers one patient has been poisoned, she does not prescribe the antidote to the entire waiting room. She treats the patient who was harmed.

The damage here was race-specific. The repair must be race-specific. Anything less is evasion dressed up as principle.

What This Looks Like

So let me be concrete, because moral arguments must lead to material change.

Reparations. Direct financial investment in Black communities and in Black families — not as charity, but as repayment. This could take the form of direct payments, baby bonds, housing grants, business capital funds, and educational trusts specifically designated for Black Americans. Multiple models exist. What has been lacking is not policy imagination but political will.

Targeted economic development. Sustained, generational investment in historically Black neighborhoods that were systematically disinvested — not gentrification that displaces, but development that empowers existing residents. Infrastructure. Schools. Hospitals. Green space. Capital.

Affirmative action with teeth. Not the tepid, loophole-ridden, constantly contested version we had, but robust, mandatory hiring and contracting goals across public and private sectors, with enforcement mechanisms, transparency requirements, and accountability.

Healthcare equity programs. Black maternal mortality is three times the white rate. Black life expectancy is shorter. These are not biological facts — they are political ones. Targeted healthcare investment, culturally competent care mandates, and the elimination of documented racial bias in treatment are not optional courtesies. They are obligations.

Criminal justice transformation. End mass incarceration, invest in community-based alternatives, eliminate cash bail, expunge records, and restore full rights — including voting rights — to every person who has served their time. And let us be honest that this system has functioned, from its inception, as a racial control mechanism.

These are not gifts. They are not special treatment. They are the minimum a society owes to people it has spent four centuries exploiting, excluding, and then blaming for the results of that exploitation and exclusion.

Addressing the Opposition

To those who say this is unfair to white Americans: I hear you. But fairness requires context.

A runner who has been shackled for twenty-six miles is not made equal by removing the shackles at mile twenty-seven and saying, "Now the race is fair." The other runners are already miles ahead. Fairness — real fairness — requires that we account for what was done.

To those who say this will breed resentment: injustice breeds resentment. Half-measures breed resentment. Telling people that their pain is imagined, that their disadvantage is their fault, that history has no consequences — that breeds resentment. Justice, even uncomfortable justice, builds a foundation that mere tolerance never can.

To those who say we cannot afford it: we could afford slavery. We could afford Jim Crow. We could afford redlining and mass incarceration. We could afford $20 trillion in stolen labor. We could afford to build the most powerful economy in human history on the backs of people we refused to pay. Do not tell me we cannot afford the remedy when we so easily afforded the crime.

To those who say it has been too long, that we should move on: debts do not expire because the debtor finds them inconvenient. Germany still pays reparations for the Holocaust. The United States paid reparations to Japanese Americans interned during World War II — forty years after the fact. The principle is established. It has simply never been applied to the nation's largest and longest crime.

The World We Are Building

I want to be clear about something. This is not about guilt. I am not asking anyone to feel guilty for what their ancestors did. Guilt is an emotion, and emotions are cheap.

I am asking for responsibility. There is a difference.

Guilt says, "I feel bad about the past." Responsibility says, "I will act to repair the present." Guilt is passive. Responsibility is a verb.

And here is what responsibility builds: it builds a nation that finally deserves the words it prints on its currency and inscribes on its monuments. It builds an economy that is stronger because it does not waste the talent of millions of people trapped by engineered disadvantage. It builds communities that are safer because they are invested in rather than surveilled. It builds children — Black children — who grow up knowing that their country sees them, values them, and has acted to prove it.

That is not a nation divided by reparative justice. That is a nation united by it — because for the first time, the promise of equality would not be a lie.

A Call to Courage

I will close with this.

Every generation faces a moral test. The test is never easy, and it is never popular at first. Abolition was not popular. Suffrage was not popular. The Civil Rights Act was not popular. In every case, the majority said: not yet, not this way, not this much, not this fast.

And in every case, history rendered its verdict. The delay was the disgrace. The action was the redemption.

We are in that moment now.

We know what was done. We know what it costs. We know what repair requires. The only question is whether we have the courage to act — not in the someday, not in the abstract, not in the watered-down, committee-approved, politically safe version — but now, fully, and without apology.

Frederick Douglass told us: "Power concedes nothing without a demand." Consider this speech a demand.

The debt is real. The damage is measurable. The remedies are known. What has been missing — the only thing that has been missing — is the will.

Let us, in this generation, find it.

Let us pay what we owe.

Let us build what we promised.

Let us, at long last, mean it when we say: liberty and justice for all.

Thank you.

Introduction

Post-emancipation, Jim Crow laws enforced segregation and disenfranchisement, while New Deal policies like the GI Bill and Federal Housing Administration loans excluded or marginalized Black veterans and families, enabling white Americans to build generational wealth through home ownership and education. In education, Black students are more likely to attend underfunded schools, face disciplinary disparities, and graduate at lower rates. Critics may claim such policies are “reverse discrimination,” but this misunderstands equity.
